detailed_answer:
The backfill answers a different question from the one the online path answers. The backfill ran today over the complete, corrected orders table, so for a transaction last March it counts every order in the 24 hours before the transaction, including orders that only arrived in the warehouse days later and excluding orders that were later cancelled and deleted. The online feature, computed at the time of the transaction, could only count orders that had arrived by then and still existed. Hence the logged online values are lower because of the late orders (deleted orders push the other way, since online counts them and the backfill does not; the observed systematic gap implies late arrivals dominate) and the backfilled values are, in this respect, cleaner than anything the live system ever sees. The model learns relationships on idealised features and meets noisier ones in production: training-serving skew caused by data availability, a form of temporal leakage, since information that was not yet known at the prediction time is used. Event-time-only correctness is not enough; the join must also respect when each record became known.

Repair. (1) Track two times per record: event time (order_ts, when it happened) and knowledge time (ingestion or loaded_at, when the system could see it), and keep history of deletions or status changes instead of overwriting. With both, the backfill can ask 'what did the table look like at time t': include a row only if loaded_at <= t and it was not yet deleted at t. (2) If history is unavailable, you cannot reproduce past knowledge exactly; use logged online feature values for the period where they exist, and for the rest consider simulating the delay (drop each order from the window with the observed delay distribution) as an approximation, flagged as such. (3) Going forward, log the features served with each prediction and use them for training and for skew checks. (4) Compare distributions of backfilled versus logged values for the same transactions before trusting any backfill, and re-evaluate the model on the logged features, which is the number that predicts production.

A related freshness point: whatever pipeline fills the online store has its own lag, and its TTL (in stores that enforce one) decides when a stale value is treated as missing; reproduce that lag in training as well, or the same kind of skew returns.
practical_answer: Worked example, hypothetical: a customer places orders at 09:00 (arrives in the warehouse immediately) and 11:00 (arrives next day at 14:00). A transaction at 12:00 is scored. Online orders_last_24h = 1, because the 11:00 order was not yet visible. The backfill run a month later returns 2. Aggregated, if 3% of orders are late and a customer averages 4 orders in the window, about 11 to 12% of customers would see a lower count online (1 - 0.97^4 is about 11.5%), which matches a systematic gap in logged versus backfilled values. Audit procedure: take 10,000 scored transactions that have logged features; recompute orders_last_24h with the as-of rule (event_ts in window, loaded_at <= transaction time, not deleted at transaction time); report the share of transactions where recomputed equals logged (target close to 100%; any remaining gap reveals other skew) versus the share where the naive backfill equals logged (expected near 88 to 89% if only late arrivals mattered; cancelled-then-deleted orders add mismatches in the opposite direction, so expect somewhat lower). Then rebuild training features with the as-of rule and re-measure offline AUC; expect it to fall toward the production figure.

detailed_answer:
Each statistic points at a different failure. The null-rate gap tells you about missing-value handling: the training data may have imputed, filtered or never contained nulls, while the live path sends them (or the reverse). The unseen-category rate detects vocabulary mismatches: spelling or case differences ('gb' vs 'GB'), new categories after the training cut-off, or a different normalisation function; those values hit the encoder's unknown-category branch, often silently mapped to a default. The L-infinity distance, the largest absolute difference in any single category's relative frequency, gives a worst-case view of distribution shift between the two samples. TensorFlow Data Validation documents expressing drift for categorical features in terms of L-infinity distance, and it supports detecting distribution skew between training and serving data; a similar statistic is a reasonable, interpretable check.

Design choices in the function: compute category frequencies over non-missing values only, so that a null-rate difference is reported separately and does not distort the frequency comparison; report which category produced the maximum gap, because 'country=gb' immediately suggests a casing bug; treat thresholds as parameters. In the test, serving sends 240 of 960 non-null values in lower case ('gb'), which the training data never contains: unseen rate 25%, L-infinity 0.25 on 'gb', and the 'GB' frequency falls from 0.60 to 0.375. 4% nulls in serving versus none in training triggers the null violation.

Limits. Sample sizes matter: with small samples, the maximum gap fluctuates by chance, so thresholds need calibrating on two training-like samples (the test checks that a 100-row sample constructed with near-training proportions, 58/31/11 against 60/30/10, does not fire at the default 0.10 threshold). The statistic is insensitive to long tails, since a thousand rare categories can each shift by little but together matter, which the unseen rate catches only for new values. It compares marginal distributions only, so a joint shift (feature relationships) goes unnoticed, and a matching distribution does not prove per-row equality: two implementations can disagree row by row yet produce the same aggregate. Row-level replay remains the definitive check.
practical_answer:
Tested implementation:

```python
from collections import Counter


def categorical_skew(train, served, linf_threshold=0.10,
                     unseen_threshold=0.01, null_gap_threshold=0.02):
    """Compare a served sample of one categorical feature with its training sample.

    None means missing. Returns a dict of statistics and a list of violations.
    linf is the largest absolute gap between category frequencies, where
    frequencies are computed over non-missing values only.
    """
    if not train or not served:
        raise ValueError("both samples must be non-empty")

    def split(values):
        present = [v for v in values if v is not None]
        return Counter(present), len(present), len(values) - len(present)

    c_tr, n_tr, miss_tr = split(train)
    c_sv, n_sv, miss_sv = split(served)
    if n_tr == 0 or n_sv == 0:
        raise ValueError("a sample has no non-missing values")

    null_tr = miss_tr / len(train)
    null_sv = miss_sv / len(served)
    gaps = {}
    for cat in set(c_tr) | set(c_sv):
        gaps[cat] = abs(c_tr[cat] / n_tr - c_sv[cat] / n_sv)
    worst_cat = min(gaps, key=lambda c: (-gaps[c], str(c)))
    linf = gaps[worst_cat]
    unseen = sum(n for cat, n in c_sv.items() if cat not in c_tr) / n_sv

    violations = []
    if abs(null_sv - null_tr) > null_gap_threshold:
        violations.append("null_rate")
    if unseen > unseen_threshold:
        violations.append("unseen_categories")
    if linf > linf_threshold:
        violations.append("linf")
    return {
        "null_rate_train": null_tr,
        "null_rate_served": null_sv,
        "linf": linf,
        "linf_category": worst_cat,
        "unseen_rate": unseen,
        "violations": violations,
    }
```

Use it on a sample of served features logged with the request id, against a sample from the training table. Start the thresholds at the defaults (0.10 on L-infinity, 1% unseen, 2 percentage points on null rate), run it on two disjoint training-like samples to see the noise floor, then tighten. Interpret violations in order: null_rate first (cheap to fix), then unseen_categories (look at the unseen values, they usually reveal normalisation bugs), then linf (look at linf_category).

code.test:
train = ["GB"] * 600 + ["US"] * 300 + ["DE"] * 100
# identical distribution -> clean
r = categorical_skew(train, list(train))
assert r["violations"] == [] and r["linf"] == 0.0 and r["unseen_rate"] == 0.0

# serving sends lower-case codes for part of the traffic and some missing values
served = ["GB"] * 360 + ["gb"] * 240 + ["US"] * 270 + ["DE"] * 90 + [None] * 40
r = categorical_skew(train, served)
assert abs(r["null_rate_train"] - 0.0) < 1e-12
assert abs(r["null_rate_served"] - 40 / 1000) < 1e-12
assert abs(r["unseen_rate"] - 240 / 960) < 1e-12
assert r["linf_category"] == "gb"
assert abs(r["linf"] - 240 / 960) < 1e-12
assert r["violations"] == ["null_rate", "unseen_categories", "linf"]

# sample-size noise alone should not fire at these thresholds
small = ["GB"] * 58 + ["US"] * 31 + ["DE"] * 11
r = categorical_skew(train, small)
assert r["violations"] == [], r

# thresholds are parameters
r = categorical_skew(train, small, linf_threshold=0.005)
assert r["violations"] == ["linf"]

for bad in ([], [None, None]):
    try:
        categorical_skew(train, bad)
    except ValueError:
        pass
    else:
        raise AssertionError("expected ValueError")
print("ok", r["linf"])
